papers.title: Short-form travel vlogs: The influence of parasocial interaction on viewers’ destination–self congruence and behavioural intention
papers.authors: Made Handijaya Dewantara, Xin Jin, and Sarah Gardiner
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: A survey experiment with 459 Australian Millennials links vlogger attractiveness, attitude homophily, and technology skill to parasocial interaction, which in turn predicts destination–self congruence, travel intention, and willingness to create electronic word of mouth. This is an adjacent mechanism study for influencer-mediated perceptions of a visited country.

papers.title: Does celebrity endorsement actually help sustainable destinations?
papers.authors: Natalia Vila-López, Isabel Pascual-Riquelme, and Ines Kuster-Boluda
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: An experiment with 432 English potential tourists compared Instagram promotion of Spain by a Spanish chef, an English chef, or no celebrity. Celebrity endorsement did not consistently outperform the control, and effects varied by familiarity and audience segment, making this an adjacent boundary-condition study for celebrity-led country image change.

papers.title: Machine translation and automatic subtitling of gender-focused messages on Instagram. A case study of a Raquel Willis’ speech
papers.category: X自动翻译 · direct platform mechanism
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: The study manually evaluates 67 English-to-Spanish subtitles automatically generated by Instagram for a gender-liberation speech. Accuracy errors were the most frequent problem, and translations often failed to preserve inclusive language, demonstrating that platform translation can expand access while distorting culturally and politically sensitive meaning.

papers.title: How Does Turning to AI for Companionship Predict Loneliness and Vice Versa?
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: A 12-month longitudinal study of more than 2,000 adults in four Western countries finds a bidirectional pattern: lower social connection predicts later increases in social-chatbot use, while increased use predicts greater loneliness on a measure of emotional isolation. The authors describe the analyses as exploratory and caution against strong causal conclusions.

papers.title: Is a random human peer better than a highly supportive chatbot in reducing loneliness over time?
papers.authors: Ruo-Ning Li, Dunigan Folk, Abhay Singh, Lyle Ungar, and Elizabeth Dunn
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: In a preregistered two-week study with 296 first-year university students, participants interacted daily with a supportive chatbot, a randomly paired human peer, or completed journaling. Human-peer interaction produced stronger loneliness benefits than the chatbot, showing that supportive AI conversation did not reproduce the cumulative benefit of reciprocal human contact.

Human-peer interaction produced stronger loneliness benefits than the chatbot, showing that supportive AI conversation did not reproduce the cumulative benefit of reciprocal human contact.

toc.title: Seeing Is Believing? Most People Struggle to Detect AI-Generated Images
toc.abstractEn: A preregistered survey experiment finds that most people distinguish photorealistic AI-generated images from authentic images only around chance level, with modest advantages for younger, analytically minded, and experienced users.

toc.title: Webs of Ainu Mosir: Indigenous Creative Networks on YouTube
toc.abstractEn: A social-network analysis examines how Ainu creators use YouTube to form Indigenous creative networks and make cultural expression visible within platformed media systems.

toc.title: Social Media Platform Repertoires in Everyday Life: Measuring Social Media Use With Passive Metering
toc.abstractEn: Passive metering is used to measure how people combine multiple social platforms in everyday repertoires, addressing limitations of self-reports and single-platform behavioral data.

toc.title: Algorithms of Injustice: An Ethnographic Content Analysis of Black Youth’s Experiences with Racial Trauma Online
toc.abstractEn: An ethnographic content analysis documents how racially traumatic social-media content affects Black youths’ well-being and how platform systems participate in the circulation of that harm.

toc.title: Automated Influence: How Social Bots Reshape Discursive Opportunities in Online Activism
toc.abstractEn: The study adapts the discursive-opportunity framework to show how social bots alter visibility, resonance, and legitimacy in online protest discourse.

toc.title: Careful Dis/Connection: Bringing Digital (Inter)Dependent Relations Out From the Shadows of Autonomy
toc.abstractEn: A conceptual analysis argues that digital disconnection should be understood through interdependence and care rather than an ideal of autonomous withdrawal from devices and platforms.

toc.title: Do Experts Agree About Misinformation? Evidence From Three Annual Surveys
toc.abstractEn: Three annual expert surveys assess agreement about the prevalence, spread, and effects of misinformation, identifying both areas of consensus and persistent uncertainty.

toc.title: Exploring the Predictors and Outcomes of Perceived Algorithm Responsiveness in Social Media Feeds: Combining Longitudinal and Computational Methods
toc.abstractEn: Longitudinal and computational analyses examine which message cues predict perceived algorithm responsiveness and how those perceptions relate to later social-media use.

toc.title: Women Sustaining TikTok as Supplementary Information Infrastructure for Flexible Work Arrangements: Gendered Conditions, Community and Surveillance
toc.abstractEn: The study examines how women use TikTok as an informal information infrastructure for interpreting flexible work, while navigating gendered community support and surveillance.

toc.title: “I Share Your Sentiment”—A Longitudinal Study of Facebook Post Sentiment and Sharing
toc.abstractEn: A population-level analysis of Norwegian political parties’ Facebook posts from 2016 to 2025 tests how negative, positive, and neutral sentiment predicts sharing over time.

toc.title: Fandom Rupture in the Movement Society: Reactive Collective Participation Through Affective Practices
toc.abstractEn: The article explains how affective practices sustain movement-like participation after an external shock draws heterogeneous fandom actors into a shared platform arena before a collective goal has formed.

papers.title: A multimodal dataset bridging brain activity, cognition, and real-world collective behavior
papers.authors: Yaling Deng, Huihong Lin, Juncheng Wu, Xiangyu Guo, Meixuan Li, Ye Wang, Hongjiang Xiao, et al.
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: This open multimodal dataset combines 64-channel EEG from 65 participants watching narrative videos with affective, cognitive, social, demographic, and psychological measures. Each stimulus is linked to real-world platform engagement such as plays, likes, comments, danmaku, saves, and shares, enabling work on narrative processing, computational social science, and neuroforecasting.

papers.title: Relationship Between Cultural Distance and Cross-Cultural Music Video Consumption on YouTube
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: Using YouTube activity around K-pop videos, national cultural dimensions, and World Bank indicators, the study tests competing cultural-proximity and cultural-exoticism accounts of cross-border media consumption. The results show that cultural distance does not operate as a single universal barrier and that its association with consumption depends on the dimension and context considered.

papers.title: A Window Into the Other Side of the World: Predictors of Viewers’ Interest in Culturally Distant Media
papers.authors: Jiyeon Yeo, Kalkidan Lea Classen, and Jan-Philipp Stein
papers.evidence: Publisher or authoritative index record verified
papers.takeaway: In a within-subject experiment with 167 Western adults, participants evaluated fictitious films framed as culturally similar or culturally distant. Openness to experience, peer interest, cultural intelligence, and learning motivation predicted interest in culturally distant media, while the broad Western versus non-Western manipulation leaves finer cultural distinctions unresolved.
